title: Electric Motor Insulation Classes: Class A, B, F and H Explained
text:
Electrical Fundamentals

 Electric Motor Insulation Classes: Class A, B, F and H Explained

 Motor insulation class defines the maximum temperature the winding insulation can withstand without degrading. Choosing the wrong class shortens motor life. Understanding it helps you specify, select, and protect motors correctly.

 
 Class A: 105°C 
 Class B: 130°C 
 Class F: 155°C 
 Class H: 180°C 
 Temperature Rise 
 




 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn about electric motor insulation classes . We will understand the four standard classes (A, B, F, H), what the temperature limits mean, how to calculate the allowable temperature rise, and how to choose the right class for your motor application.


 Every motor nameplate carries an insulation class letter that tells you the maximum temperature the winding can survive.

 Running above this limit causes exponential insulation degradation. The 10-degree rule states that every 10°C above the rated limit halves the insulation life.


 
 
 

 The 4 Standard Motor Insulation Classes


 
 
 A

 Max 105°C

 Rise: 60°C at 40°C ambient. Cotton, silk, paper. Now rare in new motors.

 

 
 B

 Max 130°C

 Rise: 80°C at 40°C ambient. Mica, glass fibre, inorganic. Standard for general-purpose motors.

 

 
 F

 Max 155°C

 Rise: 105°C at 40°C ambient. Synthetic resins, glass fibre. Most common class in modern industrial motors.

 

 
 H

 Max 180°C

 Rise: 125°C at 40°C ambient. Silicone resins, mica. Used in high ambient, VFD, and duty-cycle applications.

 Temperature Budget: How Class, Rise and Margin Add Up


 The insulation class limit is built from three components: ambient temperature + allowable temperature rise + hot-spot allowance. Understanding this budget shows how much thermal margin is left for overloads.

 Did You Know? The 10-degree rule for insulation life means that every 10°C above the rated class limit halves the insulation's expected service life. A Class F motor (rated to 155°C) running continuously at 165°C will have half the expected winding life. At 175°C it will have one-quarter the life. This is why even small, sustained overloads are disproportionately damaging to motor insulation, and why the thermal overload relay is the most important motor protection device.

 Right vs Wrong Insulation Class Selection


 
 
 Correct Selection

 
 Class F or H for VFD-driven motors (harmonic heating)

 Class H when ambient exceeds 40°C

 Class H for intermittent duty or frequent starts

 Class F minimum for all new industrial installations

 Insulation class checked against actual measured winding temperature

 
 

 
 Common Mistakes

 
 Class B motor used on VFD (harmonic losses push winding above 130°C)

 Class A or B in high-ambient enclosures (ambient alone may exceed rise budget)

 Assuming Class F nameplate rating means the motor runs at 155°C (it runs cooler)

 Ignoring service factor SF 1.15 means motor can run at 115% load, not 115% temperature

 Using Class B motor as direct replacement for failed Class F without checking thermal margin

 
 




 Tip: Using a Class F motor with Class B temperature rise gives a 25°C thermal margin. 

Many modern motors are designed with Class F insulation but specified to run with Class B temperature rise (80°C rise at 40°C ambient). This means the winding only reaches 120°C in normal operation, but the insulation is rated to 155°C. The 35°C margin extends motor life significantly and handles overloads, high ambient, or harmonic heating without risk. This practice is called Class F insulation with Class B rise.
